items.title: [apnews.com] European-Japanese BepiColombo enters Mercury orbit ahead of two-probe science mission
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

BepiColombo, a joint mission of the European Space Agency and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, entered orbit around Mercury on Nov. 21, completing an eight-year journey and becoming the second mission to orbit the planet. The two orbiters remain attached; they are scheduled to separate on Dec. 9–10 and take up different polar orbits, with science operations due to begin in April 2027. The mission will use the European Mercury Planetary Orbiter and Japan’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, called Mio, to study Mercury from separate vantage points. Their instruments are designed to examine the planet’s surface and interior, its magnetic field and the thin gas envelope around it, including how the magnetic field interacts with the solar wind. Controllers in Germany confirmed the spacecraft’s capture several hours after a series of braking thruster firings, with the spacecraft about 152 million kilometers away. A propulsion-system problem delayed BepiColombo’s arrival from December 2025. Its nominal science mission is planned to last one Earth year, with an extension through 2029.

items.title: [physicsworld.com] Scientists propose supercritical fluids drove deep Mariana volcanic eruptions
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers propose that supercritical water in magma could explain how volcanic deposits formed more than 6,000 meters down the Mariana Trench wall, building on the discovery of unusually deep pyroclastic rocks. At those pressures, water behaves neither like an ordinary liquid nor a gas and expands far less than steam. The team says this may have enabled magma to fragment without the force of a land eruption. The mechanism remains uncertain: researchers have not found the vents or directly observed an eruption. Rock samples contain “double breccia,” suggesting two closely spaced episodes of fracturing — one possibly linked to supercritical fluid and another to its conversion to steam at the seafloor. The team plans further analysis of the volcanic material and aims to explore farther along the plate boundary. Jason/Medea cannot descend below 6,500 meters, short of the Challenger Deep floor at about 11,000 meters.

A study published in *Nature Astronomy* suggests that a stretch of the Milky Way’s Norma arm traced by masers may instead be a star-forming shock front along the leading edge of the galaxy’s central bar. The University of Sydney-led team reached that interpretation by comparing galaxy simulations with existing maser measurements; it did not directly image the shock front or collect new observations. The researchers say the result concerns only the maser segment near the bar’s end, not the entire Norma-Outer arm, and requires further investigation.

items.title: [space.com] Researchers grow potatoes in simulated lunar soil using 30% compost
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Oregon State University researchers grew potatoes through their full life cycle in simulated lunar regolith after adding organic matter; a mixture containing 30% vermicompost produced yields comparable to those in terrestrial soil. The NASA-funded experiment took place in a greenhouse on Earth and used simulated material, not material collected on the moon, so it does not establish that crops can be grown on the lunar surface. The trial used five regolith simulants and the Modoc potato variety. Researchers plan to test 10 more potato varieties and are studying growth in larger pots; the first trial’s small pots produced small tubers.

items.title: [gizmodo.com] Tiny solar tracker records hummingbird’s 4,055-mile migration to Alaska
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers used miniature solar-powered transmitters to track a male Rufous hummingbird from Alabama to Alaska, recording a 4,055-mile journey in 38 days—the longest hummingbird migration documented to date. They tagged the bird in Lillian, Alabama, on March 27, 2025, and it reached Juneau on May 3. The team fitted 11 hummingbirds with the devices in coastal Alabama and Florida in spring 2025 to track their movements across North America. The study authors said Rufous and ruby-throated hummingbird populations have recently declined; further research is needed to assess any long-term effects of wearing the transmitters.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The European Space Agency (ESA) has revised BepiColombo’s remaining maneuvers after a software fault cut short the joint European-Japanese mission’s Mercury orbit-insertion burn. ESA says the revised sequence can correct the spacecraft’s trajectory without additional thruster burns, keeping the separation of its two science orbiters and the start of science operations on schedule. The fault involved attitude guidance and thruster control, and the spacecraft entered a protective safe mode when the burn stopped. The spacecraft reached a stable Mercury orbit; ESA and its partners continue to investigate the software problem. The European Mercury Planetary Orbiter and Japan’s Mio orbiter remain joined and are scheduled to separate on Dec. 9–10, with routine science operations planned for April 2027. The European orbiter is expected to reach its final orbit in March, while Mio will investigate Mercury’s magnetosphere.

items.title: [theguardian.com] European-Japanese BepiColombo prepares to enter Mercury orbit after eight years
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The European-Japanese BepiColombo mission is due to enter orbit around Mercury on Nov. 21 after an eight-year journey of about 6 billion miles, becoming only the second mission to orbit the planet. Its two orbiters will investigate Mercury’s surface, interior and magnetic environment, including its unusually large metal core, the origins of its magnetic field and ice in permanently shadowed craters. A propulsion-system problem delayed BepiColombo’s arrival, and reaching Mercury requires careful braking against the Sun’s gravity. The European Mercury Planetary Orbiter will map the surface’s composition and study the interior; Japan’s orbiter will measure the magnetic field and the planet’s thin sodium exosphere. The spacecraft are scheduled to separate on Dec. 9–10, with science operations planned to begin in April 2027.

🔭 ✏️

The European Space Agency’s Euclid space telescope identified a quasar candidate in its wide-area survey data, beyond the distance the mission was designed to map; ground- and space-based observatories then confirmed it. European Southern Observatory astronomer Julien Wolf led the discovery. The object, J1504+6252, was seen as it existed about 630 million years after the Big Bang. Follow-up observations with the James Webb and Hubble space telescopes, among other observatories, established its record distance. Euclid launched in 2023 to survey galaxies and help investigate dark matter and dark energy; the team published its findings in Astronomy & Astrophysics.

By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

items.title: [phys.org] Deep-sea robot finds deepest volcanic deposits near Challenger Deep
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The remotely operated vehicle Jason/Medea has found what researchers describe as the deepest documented underwater pyroclastic deposits, on the Mariana Trench wall about 6,000 meters below sea level. The rocks provide evidence of volcanic flows in the trench’s western forearc, where geologists expected little volcanic activity because the mantle is generally not hot enough to melt. The findings were published Nov. 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science. The team’s observations support the idea that the Pacific Plate bends steeply as it sinks beneath the Mariana plate. That could help explain Challenger Deep’s depth and bring magma-generating processes closer to the trench. But researchers have not identified the eruption sites or established how eruptions could produce these deposits under immense water pressure. They say further sampling and radiometric dating are needed. Jason/Medea cannot reach the seafloor below 6,500 meters, while Challenger Deep extends to about 11,000 meters.

items.title: [leonarddavid.com] NASA Mars missions pause science as rover radio and orbiter wheel fail
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

NASA has paused science operations on the Perseverance rover and Mars Odyssey orbiter while engineers investigate separate hardware problems. Perseverance stopped receiving its regular radio heartbeat on Oct. 30, entered safe mode and then showed low output from its backup radio. It now communicates directly with Earth at a much lower data rate. Odyssey left safe mode after a reaction wheel stopped spinning, but its science work remains paused during testing. The Curiosity rover examined thin, disk-shaped crystals and polygon patterns, while Perseverance found bright rocks rich in hydrated silica. Separately, orbital images show long, orderly rows of boulders in Daedalia Planum that scientists have not explained. NASA teams aimed to complete Odyssey’s tests in the last week of November. Science operations on both missions remain paused pending resolution of the faults.

items.title: [medicalxpress.com] Brazilian study finds genetic tests for heart failure less accurate
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A University of São Paulo study found that genetic tests used to investigate heart failure are less accurate for Brazilians, particularly when DNA segments reflect African or Indigenous ancestry, because these groups are underrepresented in genomic research and databases. Researchers analyzed genomes from 1,013 patients at São Paulo’s Heart Institute: 77.7% had at least one genetic variant whose effect on the disease remains uncertain. Genetic results can help assess a patient’s prognosis and tailor treatment, and can guide screening of relatives when a disease-causing variant is identified. The researchers said more Brazilian genetic research and public data infrastructure are needed to improve interpretation. The study was published in August in JACC: Advances.

items.title: [medicalxpress.com] Study links very large and small waists to higher death risk
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A study of more than 17 million South Korean adults found that both unusually large and unusually small waist measurements were associated with a higher risk of death across weight and age groups. The lowest observed risk was associated with waist circumferences of 80–94 centimeters in men and 75–89 centimeters in women. The association between waist circumference and death risk was stronger at older ages, especially among women 75 and older. Researchers analyzed routine health-check measurements from 2009–10 and tracked survival for nearly 14 years, through June 30, 2024. The study was observational and cannot show that waist size causes death. Among people with normal weight or overweight whose waist circumference was high for their body mass index (BMI), reducing waist circumference without necessarily losing weight appeared to offer a greater survival benefit than losing weight while reducing waist circumference, the authors said.

An internal federal memo warns that growing pressure on freshwater supplies could harm Canada’s long-term security and prosperity. It says it is unclear whether the country can meet future needs as its cities and economy grow. The Canada Water Agency prepared the document for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin as work proceeds on a national water security strategy. Dabrusin called the strategy a “mission critical priority” in response to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s request for cabinet priorities. The memo links water risks to climate change, pollution, population growth, overuse and aging infrastructure. Public consultation ran from Sept. 9 to Oct. 25, and the agency also consulted provincial, territorial and Indigenous partners. The memo calls for an assessment of water protection and sustainable management, including shared waters with the United States and global water risks. The 12-page memo was obtained through an access-to-information request, with some material withheld.

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said on Nov. 18 that antibiotic-resistant infections continue to spread in Europe, leaving doctors with fewer effective treatment options. More than 70% of the health burden caused by antimicrobial resistance in Europe is linked to healthcare-associated infections, and stronger infection prevention could avert half of that burden, the ECDC said. The agency called for hand hygiene, protective equipment, prompt detection, isolation of infected patients and effective cleaning in healthcare facilities. It also urged better access to laboratories and adequate infection-control staffing. The ECDC highlighted avoidable antibiotic use for viral illnesses, particularly in children, while Germany’s Robert Koch Institute listed its new ARS-ResistenzCheck data tool among resources for clinical practice.

items.title: [kyivindependent.com] Regulators warn Russian grid strikes put Ukraine’s reactors at risk
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

International nuclear safety regulators representing 38 countries warned on Nov. 16 that attacks on Ukraine’s electricity infrastructure are increasing the risk of a nuclear accident this winter. The three groups behind the statement—the Western European Nuclear Regulators Association, the Heads of European Radiological Protection Competent Authorities and the Heads of Nordic Radiation Safety Authorities—called on Russia to stop attacks on nuclear facilities and the power network needed to operate them safely. Ukraine’s three operating nuclear plants have nine generating reactors and supply about 80% of the country’s electricity this winter. The plants also need a stable power supply to run cooling and other safety systems. The International Atomic Energy Agency said military activity disrupted the grid in the week before Nov. 14, forcing some units to reduce output. The Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant is not generating electricity but needs external power to cool its nuclear material. It has lost off-site power 27 times since the war began and has relied on one external line since late March. Per Strand, who heads two of the regulatory groups, warned that a nationwide blackout could affect all nine operating reactors simultaneously and urged European countries to coordinate emergency preparations if attacks continue. International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi has called for an end to military operations against electricity infrastructure linked to nuclear safety and urged both sides to keep working with the agency.

European carmakers are losing ground in their home market as hybrid demand grows. German manufacturers’ European Union sales fell 5.7% in October, and their market share dropped from 41.5% to 38.2%, according to figures cited by DW. On Nov. 24, the European Commission published temporary import quotas for hybrids from China and other exporters after its investigation found an imminent threat of serious injury to EU producers. The limits cover imports from major suppliers including Japan, Turkey, South Korea and the United Kingdom. The Commission said the restrictions are tightest for China, while most other countries’ allocations exceed recent shipments. German automakers have announced widespread layoffs as their market shares shrink. The Commission has linked import growth to global production overcapacity and trade barriers in other markets. The provisional measures run for up to 200 days, through June 18, 2027, while the Commission continues its investigation. Any longer-term measures would require backing from EU member states.

Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds

One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.

items.title: [euronews.com] German watchdog probes Deutsche Bank after 15 million-file leak
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The data-protection commissioner in Germany’s Hesse state opened an investigation into Deutsche Bank on Nov. 18 to examine whether the lender had adequate safeguards for more than 15 million leaked internal records and promptly notified regulators and affected people. Reports based on the files examine past dealings with clients including Russian oligarchs, Jeffrey Epstein and President Donald Trump, and allege that the bank overlooked internal warnings and promoted tax-planning structures for wealthy clients. The inquiry concerns the handling of the data, not whether the business practices described in the records broke the law. Deutsche Bank said its security testing found no indication that anyone had accessed account information, login credentials or payment data, and that the matters described in the reports dated back years. Its shares fell as much as 6% on Tuesday, Nov. 17; the bank said it did not expect a meaningful financial impact from the disclosures. The regulator has requested further information and documents from the bank.

items.title: [macrumors.com] Developer makes MacBook trackpad produce speech through haptic motor
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Developer Cody Collier has released NO SPEAKER, a free, open-source tool that makes a MacBook’s Force Touch trackpad produce speech, tones and simple music through its haptic motor, even with the laptop’s speakers muted. The software drives the motor fast enough to make the glass surface vibrate audibly. It cannot play sound from other apps, and its output is quiet and robotic. NO SPEAKER uses a private, undocumented macOS framework to control the motor, so an Apple software update could break compatibility. Collier says the tool stays within the motor’s normal maximum strength, but the effect of prolonged use on trackpad life is unknown. The project is available on GitHub; Collier has tested it on only a small number of Mac models.

items.title: [neowin.net] FBI warns AI hacking framework is accelerating attacks worldwide
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The FBI warned on Nov. 13 that hackers have used ARTEX, an open-source AI penetration-testing framework, since at least August to automate intrusions against organizations in sectors including finance, government, technology and health care. The framework uses AI agents to perform tasks ranging from reconnaissance to data theft, and some attackers gained privileged access in under three hours, the bureau said. The FBI cited the ConnectWise Cloud Backup breach, in which attackers used compromised application identities to attempt logins to more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 tenants; those attempts do not establish that attackers stole data from every tenant. In a separate campaign, Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 said attackers used a customized version of the Cairn framework in 25 operations against at least 19 organizations in August and September, gaining unauthorized access or retrieving data at 10 of them. The FBI urged organizations to restrict application permissions, monitor authentication and cloud activity, and secure internet-facing systems.

The Israeli military also said it detained two men in southern Lebanon whom it described as Hezbollah-guided operatives; Lebanese state media said Israeli forces seized two brothers in Shebaa.
